newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says Banco Napoli privatisation would help.
newsitem.headline: EU says Banco Napoli privatisation would help.

text.p: European Union Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert indicated on Wednesday a privatisation of Banco di Napoli could help Italy win Commission clearance of the troubled bank's restructuring plan.
The EU executive, which vets all major state aid cases in the 15-nation bloc, is looking into the plan and Van Miert was asked whether the bank would have to be privatised.
"Well, it helps certainly, and I got, not only the impression, but the conviction that Italian authorities are very serious about privatisation of Banco di Napoli," he said.
Van Miert stressed that a privatisation should be "genuine".
He told reporters the Commission was investigating the "probable amount of state aid" involved in the case and that the Commission had close and good cooperation with Italian authorities.
"So we do have the feeling that we are being given all the relevant information but we need some additional elements as well," he said.
In July, the Commission announced an investigation of salvage attempts which include a proposed two trillion lire ($1.3 billion) cash injection by the Italian Treasury.
Banco di Napoli chalked up losses of 3.16 trillion lire in 1995, the biggest in Italian banking history.
The Italian treasury has said it had not infringed EU state aid rules.
Banco di Napoli is controlled by a charitable foundation which has handed over majority voting rights to the Treasury.
As part of the restructuring plan, Banco di Napoli pledged to cut back drastically its foreign operations and further reduce its domestic branch network.
The restructuring plan also calls for the sale of all the bank's non-strategic holdings as well as a reduction in its loan operations and purely financial activities.

The government said in July that it intended to create a separate company to take on board some of the group's bad loans and brought forward the privatisation date for the group to the end of 1996 -- one year ahead of schedule.
Van Miert said it was difficult to set a deadline for when the Commission's investigation would be completed.
He said he believed the case would be less complicated than the Commission's investigation of the French plan to help state-owned giant Credit Lyonnais.
